title: Resistors in Combination
notes: Resistors in series carry the same current. The total voltage is the sum of the voltages, so the equivalent resistance is R = R1 + R2 + R3. The equivalent is larger than the largest single resistor.
Resistors in parallel have the same potential difference. The total current is the sum of the branch currents, so 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. The equivalent is smaller than the smallest branch.
Two parallel resistors have the shortcut R = R1 R2 / (R1 + R2). It is the product over the sum, and it is not used for three resistors without grouping.
A short string of series resistors can sit in parallel with another branch. Reduce the series string first, then combine the parallel pair.
The voltage divider is the series case: the larger resistor takes the larger share of the voltage, in proportion to its resistance, because the current is common.
Opening a parallel branch increases the equivalent resistance and decreases the total current from the source. Adding a parallel branch does the opposite.
confusion: ❌ 'Adding resistors in parallel increases the total resistance.' ✅ Parallel connections *decrease* total resistance, as they provide more paths for current to flow (1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2).
❌ 'In series, current changes across each resistor.' ✅ In a series circuit, the *current* remains the same through all components, while *voltage* splits proportionally.

❌ 'Total resistance in series is the average of individual resistances.' ✅ In series, the total resistance is the *sum* of individual resistances (Rs = R1 + R2), which is always greater than the largest individual resistor.
Parallel resistors do not add their ohm values.
The product-over-sum rule is for two resistors only.
Series current is the same. Series voltage is not.
A parallel equivalent is never larger than the smaller branch.
